provenance.label: SYNTHETIC / DEMO-ONLY
provenance.description: All initiatives, evidence references, dates, owners, prices, and issue drafts are fictional planning material created for a Copilot-for-Product demo.
limitations: No item is a shopper, seller, or production commitment.
Evidence is deliberately small, invented, and contradictory.
Targets are proposed decision aids rather than measured baselines.
Human decision flags must not be resolved automatically.

horizons.label: Now
horizons.definition: Active discovery and preview-hardening work through September 2026; timing is illustrative.

horizons.label: Next
horizons.definition: Gated options for October through December 2026, entered only after explicit evidence and risk review.

horizons.label: Later
horizons.definition: Uncommitted opportunities for 2027 or later; sequence and scope remain open.

evidenceReferences.summary: A fictional collector repeatedly rebuilds the same narrow chase-card search.
A synthetic participant prioritizes explanation when catalog taxonomy changes.
An occasional buyer questions whether Saved Searches is relevant.

Removed expansion values require explicit recovery.
Apply, update, and save-as-new semantics need separation.
Synthetic later-session reuse is directional, not causal.

risks.mitigation: Repeat clear device-local language at create and manage surfaces.

issueDraft.title: [Synthetic demo] Harden browser-local Saved Searches preview
issueDraft.body:
## Outcome
Make personal Saved Searches reliable, understandable, and accessible while keeping them explicitly device-local.

## Evidence
Review the synthetic references on initiative `init-saved-searches-preview`; they include repeat-use signals and counter-signals about reach, stale taxonomy, sync expectations, and alert consent.

## Boundaries
No account sync, price alerts, listing snapshots, card images, or sensitive telemetry. Human decisions remain open.

## Done when
Core flows meet the approved acceptance boundary, corrupt state is recoverable, stale criteria are explained, and saving never implies notification consent.

childWorkItems.title: Version and validate local search records
acceptanceCriteria: Unsupported or corrupt records cannot block the card catalog.
Stored records exclude listing snapshots, prices, card identities, and alert consent.

childWorkItems.title: Complete create, apply, rename, and delete flows
acceptanceCriteria: Device-local persistence is explained during creation and management.
Active and edited states are distinct without relying on color.

childWorkItems.title: Explain stale expansion and rarity criteria
acceptanceCriteria: Unavailable criteria are never silently substituted.
The shopper can review, update, or delete an invalid search.

childWorkItems.title: Validate keyboard, screen-reader, reflow, and status behavior
acceptanceCriteria: Core flows work without pointer input.
Save, apply, and recovery outcomes are programmatically announced.

initiatives.title: Make listing trust signals easier to compare
initiatives.outcome: Shoppers can compare price, condition, seller reputation, and market context without mistaking any one signal for a guarantee.

evidenceReferences.summary: A fictional shopper weighs condition and seller history alongside price.
A synthetic collector prioritizes explanation over shortcut speed.
Generic collectible marketplaces emphasize condition, seller, and price context.

risks.description: Dense badges and metadata could make listings harder to scan.
risks.mitigation: Test hierarchy and progressive disclosure across expertise levels.

risks.description: A market comparison could be mistaken for an appraisal or guaranteed resale value.
risks.mitigation: Use contextual language, freshness labels, and explicit synthetic-demo boundaries.

humanDecisionFlags.question: Which trust signals must remain visible in every listing card?

successMeasures.criterion: Synthetic participants can explain price, condition, seller, and market context without prompting.
Zero participants interpret market context as a guaranteed appraisal.

issueDraft.title: [Synthetic demo] Prototype comparable card listing trust signals
issueDraft.body:
## Outcome
Help shoppers compare condition, seller reputation, price, and market context without overclaiming authenticity or value.

## Scope
Test information hierarchy, contextual language, and responsive behavior. No real grading, authentication, seller scoring, or pricing integration.

childWorkItems.title: Define listing signal hierarchy and language
acceptanceCriteria: Price, condition, seller, and market language has a documented hierarchy.
No content implies guaranteed authenticity or resale value.

childWorkItems.title: Prototype listing comparison across viewports
acceptanceCriteria: Core trust context remains readable at 320 CSS px.
The listing can be understood with keyboard and screen reader.

initiatives.title: Evaluate account-synced Saved Searches
initiatives.outcome: The team can decide whether cross-device continuity merits durable account storage without conflating it with price alerts.

evidenceReferences.summary: One fictional ticket expected a saved search on another device.
Directional later-session reuse does not establish cross-device need.
A synthetic collector checks saved hunts on mobile after creating them on desktop.

risks.description: Durable storage creates migration, retention, export, deletion, and support obligations.
risks.mitigation: Complete architecture, privacy, and lifecycle review before an experiment.

risks.description: Cross-device infrastructure may not address why most synthetic shoppers did not save a search.
risks.mitigation: Require qualitative cross-device evidence and a bounded experiment plan.

humanDecisionFlags.question: Has the local preview met the reliability and reuse gate for a sync experiment?
What retention, deletion, export, and migration policy applies to saved criteria?

successMeasures.criterion: A bounded synthetic study demonstrates a meaningful workflow that local storage cannot support.
Privacy, security, retention, deletion, export, and migration owners explicitly approve the experiment.

issueDraft.title: [Synthetic demo] Evaluate account sync for Saved Searches
issueDraft.body:
## Decision to make
Determine whether evidence justifies a bounded cross-device Saved Searches experiment.

## Gate
Do not implement until local reliability, accessibility, privacy, retention, deletion, export, and migration questions have named owners and explicit approval. This does not include price alerts.

childWorkItems.title: Study cross-device search continuity
acceptanceCriteria: Research distinguishes cross-session from cross-device reuse.
Counter-signals and occasional-buyer workflows are documented.

childWorkItems.title: Define storage and data-lifecycle options
acceptanceCriteria: Options cover migration, export, retention, deletion, and conflict handling.
Security and privacy reviewers record unresolved risks.

childWorkItems.title: Record the sync experiment decision
acceptanceCriteria: Decision cites evidence and rejected alternatives.
No automatic launch follows from a metric threshold.

initiatives.title: Research explicit price-drop alerts
initiatives.outcome: Collectors can evaluate an opt-in alert concept without treating every saved search as notification consent or stale inventory as actionable.

evidenceReferences.summary: A fictional repeat collector would value a narrowly targeted alert.
Price alone does not determine purchase intent.
One fictional request asks for a threshold-based near-mint alert.
Generic search alerts combine criteria with price thresholds.
Notification products expose explicit channel, cadence, pause, and unsubscribe controls.

risks.description: Saving a search could be mistaken for consent to receive notifications.
risks.mitigation: Require separate opt-in with explicit threshold, channel, cadence, and unsubscribe.

risks.description: A card may sell or change condition before the shopper opens an alert.
risks.mitigation: Define freshness and sold-inventory behavior before delivery prototyping.

humanDecisionFlags.question: Which price-monitoring job is frequent and valuable enough to justify notifications?
What constitutes explicit consent and who controls frequency?

successMeasures.criterion: Synthetic participants distinguish saving from subscribing and can identify threshold, channel, cadence, and unsubscribe.
Zero; every delivery path has separate explicit consent.

issueDraft.title: [Synthetic demo] Research opt-in price-drop alerts
issueDraft.body:
## Question
Would a separately configured price alert help repeat collectors, and can it remain clearly distinct from Saved Searches?

## Guardrails
Saving is never notification consent. Define threshold, freshness, sold-inventory behavior, channel, cadence, quiet hours, pause, and unsubscribe before implementation.

childWorkItems.title: Study collector price-monitoring jobs
acceptanceCriteria: Research distinguishes exact-card thresholds from broad inventory monitoring.
Counter-signals and non-alert alternatives are documented.

childWorkItems.title: Define explicit alert preferences and lifecycle
acceptanceCriteria: Save and subscribe remain separate actions.
Threshold, channel, cadence, quiet hours, pause, and unsubscribe are covered.

childWorkItems.title: Define price freshness and sold-inventory behavior
acceptanceCriteria: Trigger inputs and freshness expectations are explicit.
Sold or changed-condition listings cannot produce a success-shaped outcome.

initiatives.title: Explore collection and wishlist lists
initiatives.outcome: The team can decide whether stable card lists solve a distinct collection-management job rather than duplicating dynamic Saved Searches.

evidenceReferences.summary: An occasional buyer needs guidance rather than another persistent personal tool.
Generic collector products distinguish stable lists from dynamic searches.

risks.description: Wishlist, binder, and search concepts could create overlapping destinations and unclear ownership state.
risks.mitigation: Define distinct jobs and data models before solution testing.

humanDecisionFlags.question: Is the primary unmet job wishlisting, collection ownership, gifting, or none?

successMeasures.criterion: Multiple observed workflows establish a job that Saved Searches cannot meet.
Zero; saving or buying never silently marks a card as owned.

issueDraft.title: [Synthetic demo] Explore collector wishlists and owned-card lists
issueDraft.body:
## Question
Do collectors need a stable wishlist or owned-card list that is meaningfully different from a dynamic Saved Search?

## Boundary
This is an uncommitted research candidate. Saving a search or adding to cart never implies ownership.

childWorkItems.title: Observe wishlist and collection-management workflows
acceptanceCriteria: Study distinguishes wishlisting, ownership, gifting, and dynamic search.
Evidence limitations and counter-signals are recorded.

childWorkItems.title: Define list concepts without ownership ambiguity
acceptanceCriteria: Candidate models specify item state, provenance, edit, archive, and delete behavior.
Save, cart, purchase, and ownership remain distinct actions.
